retrieval_text: An 88-year-old female was found lying down. Upon admission, she exhibited nausea, vomiting, altered mental status, and a slow heart rate. Her medical history includes essential hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, hypothyroidism, chronic renal failure (Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes G3a classification), ischemic stroke, and osteoporosis.

A 27-year-old male patient presented for refractive surgery with no reported medical or ocular history. His manifest refraction was −3.00 −1.50 × 90 in the right eye and −4.75 DS in the left eye, with a corrected distance visual acuity (CDVA) of 20/15 in both eyes. Examination revealed a 2.5 mm × 3 mm paracentral nummular scar in the corneal stroma at the 2 o'clock position in the right eye. After obtaining informed consent, an uneventful LASIK procedure was performed using the AMO IntraLase femtosecond laser. Flap diameters were 8.4 mm in the right eye and 8.3 mm in the left eye, with a thickness of 100 μm. The optical zone was 6.5 mm with a transitional zone of 1.25 mm in both eyes, using the WaveLight EX500 Excimer Laser.

A 21-year-old male visited the orthopedic outpatient department with a history of left hip pain persisting for 1 year after a minor fall. The patient reported difficulty in performing heavy strenuous activities such as running, jumping, and other sports activities. Pain was noted at the terminal range of movements. The FABER test yielded a positive result. The patient was able to actively raise his leg.

A 13-year-old male student presented with a flattening of the right anterior chest wall since birth. He had no symptoms other than cosmetic concerns. He was the second child in his family, with no similar presentations or associated familial disorders reported. Physical examination showed normal growth parameters and IQ. There were no abnormal craniofacial findings. The chest wall was asymmetric with underdevelopment on the right side. The patient exhibited normal strength in the right upper limb and a full range of motion in the shoulder joint. Both limbs were symmetric with no finger anomalies. Auscultation of the chest revealed normal heart sounds, breath sounds, and respiration pattern.

A 1-month-old male infant was brought in with a swelling located in the occipital region, which had been present since birth. The parents reported that the swelling had gradually increased in size to its current dimensions of 14 cm × 12 cm. The affected area featured dysplastic skin and was encircled by a ring of coarse hair. The lesion had a cystic appearance and contained clear fluid. It was compressible, nonpulsatile, transilluminant, and its size and tension remained unchanged regardless of the infant's position or crying.

A 25-year-old male came for an eye examination due to a gradual decrease in visual acuity in his left eye over the past few years. The patient and his family noted that he had difficulty fixating with the left eye since early childhood. He sought medical attention hoping for improvement. There was no history of trauma, ocular surgery, or any other interventions. The family confirmed that his vision had been poor since childhood. On physical examination, the patient exhibited distinctive facial and body features. There were areas of hypopigmented hair on both forearms. Facial features included synophrys, a high nasal root, a prominent nasal root, and a white forelock of hair. Oral examination revealed a high-arched palate with dental anomalies such as microdontia, oligodontia, and conical teeth. The patient had no hearing deficits, and there was no relevant family history. Examination also showed lateral displacement of the inner canthi (dystopia canthorum).

A 47-year-old female visited for a routine dental checkup. Since birth, she had multiple discrete purple discolorations on the right side of her chin, neck, and lower limb. She reported experiencing blurred vision for the past year. General examination showed stable vital signs. Extraoral examination revealed facial asymmetry on the right side due to soft tissue hypertrophy, with numerous discrete purple lesions on the right frontal region of the face, eyelid, around the nose, chin, and lips. These lesions extended to the back of the neck and shoulder, not crossing the midline. Intraoral examination showed asymptomatic bright-red flat areas of discoloration present from birth on the right postero-lateral border of the hard palate, extending laterally 1.5 cm from the palatal aspect of the free or marginal gingiva near the 17 tooth region, medially 2 cm from the mid-palatine raphe region, posteriorly to the right posterolateral junction of the hard and soft palate, and on the right ventral surface of the floor of the mouth near the lingual aspect of the 44, 45, and 46 tooth regions. The right lateral border of the tongue was also bright red and enlarged. Similar purplish lesions were observed on the flexor and extensor aspects of the right lower limb. The skin lesions were flat, non-elevated, and purplish in color, while the oral lesions were bright red due to the presence of oxygenated blood in fine capillaries.

A seven-month-old male presented with an eye turn since birth. Examination revealed esotropia at near measuring 60 prism-diopters, alternate fixation with a preference for the right eye, and -4 abduction in both eyes. Cycloplegic refraction was +1.50 diopters in both eyes, and the rest of the ophthalmic examination was unremarkable. Surgical intervention included a 6mm medial rectus muscle recession in both eyes and a 6mm lateral rectus resection in the left eye. One week after surgery, the patient exhibited orthotropia with a palpebral fissure in the left eye that was 1 mm narrower than that of the right eye.

A 42-year-old Caucasian woman, employed as a nurse, presented with an elevated alanine transaminase concentration of 469 U/L (normal range: 10-35) during an evaluation for sub-fertility. Other liver function tests, including albumin levels and coagulation screen, were within normal limits. She exhibited no symptoms or signs indicative of liver disease. Her medical history included recurrent urinary tract infections and previous miscarriages. She was taking folic acid and nitrofurantoin 50 mg daily for the past two years. There was no reported history of excessive alcohol consumption or use of herbal remedies or supplements. Physical examination did not reveal any abnormalities.

A 10-day-old, full-term Caucasian male infant was admitted to a local hospital with symptoms of viral gastroenteritis. During the hospital stay, pediatric surgical services were consulted due to left scrotal swelling, and a left hydrocele was identified. The patient was subsequently discharged. Seventeen days later, at four weeks of age, the infant returned with a 24-hour history of left scrotal swelling, redness, fever, and a pus-like discharge from an ulcerated area in the left hemi-scrotum. An abdominal examination showed normal results, while a scrotal examination revealed a left scrotal abscess and a hard, swollen left testis. No hernia was detected. Immediate surgical exploration was planned. Intravenous antibiotics (amoxicillin with clavulanic acid and flucloxacillin) and fluids were administered due to the local scrotal infection. A midline raphe scrotal incision was performed, and a small amount of pus was drained. Necrotic scrotal wall tissue was excised back to healthy tissue margins. The tunica vaginalis was noted to be thickened, and the testis was found to be edematous with a normal blood supply. No evidence of testicular torsion was observed. The wound was thoroughly washed with antiseptic solution, and the dartos muscle and skin were closed using absorbable sutures. The fever subsided shortly after surgery, and the swelling, redness, and pain decreased over the next 48 hours.

A 52-year-old African American man presented with a history of subcutaneous nodules appearing across various parts of his body and a noticeable reduction in subcutaneous fat. These symptoms emerged twelve years after an initial episode at the age of 34, during which similar nodules were observed but resolved without intervention.

A 6-year-old female presented with a four-week history of headache and vomiting. The headache was gradual in onset, dull in nature, primarily on the left side, and more severe in the morning, with vomiting providing relief. Additionally, she experienced difficulty with walking. Neurological examination revealed a fully conscious child with normal higher cerebral functions. She exhibited truncal ataxia, but other cerebellar functions were intact. Examination of other systems showed no abnormalities.

A 10-year-old girl was brought to the hospital due to issues with her visual field. She had been experiencing worsening headaches, nausea, and weight loss over the past six months. Her medical history and family history were unremarkable. Upon admission, she was initially thought to have gastroenteritis. However, she later developed abducens nerve palsy in her left eye along with visual field disturbances.

A 54-year-old Japanese woman presented to the outpatient clinic with a 20-year history of subcutaneous fat loss on her left upper limb. She has been receiving treatment for hypothyroidism for 22 years and for chronic rheumatoid arthritis for 11 years. There is no family history of similar conditions. Physical examination at the initial visit showed multifocal subcutaneous fat loss on both upper limbs, shoulders, back, abdomen, and the left lower limb.

The patient is a 5-year-old girl from Bihar, India, born to nonconsanguineous parents with a normal perinatal period. She remained healthy until 40 months of age when she experienced acute onset lethargy and confusion following an upper respiratory tract infection, which resolved spontaneously over 5 days. During recovery, she exhibited rapid involuntary eye movements, tremulous hand and finger movements, and an unsteady gait. The gait instability gradually improved, and she regained the ability to walk without falling. Over the next 3 months, she had two episodes of febrile illness with transient increases in gait unsteadiness. At 48 months, she experienced febrile encephalopathy with seizures and was bedridden for 10 days before returning to baseline. She was then started on oral valproic acid. At 54 months, she developed slowly progressive hearing loss. At 60 months, she presented with the ability to walk without support, speak in two-word sentences, dress and undress, and feed herself. There was no history of visual impairment or similar illnesses in her family. Examination at 60 months revealed normal anthropometry, left convergent squint, horizontal nystagmus, bilateral pale optic discs, hypotonia, areflexia, and perioral and appendicular dyskinesia (intermittent spontaneous jerky movements of fingers, toes, limbs, and lips). Cerebellar examination showed gait incoordination (gait ataxia), truncal hypotonia, intentional tremors, positive finger-nose test, dysdiadochokinesia, and incoordinated slurred speech (scanning speech). Pes cavus was not present.

A 61-year-old male reported experiencing a painful mass in the left epididymis for several months. There was no fever or history of trauma associated with the condition. Hematological parameters and urine indexes were found to be within normal limits. Urine culture showed no bacterial growth.

A 66-year-old female with a medical history of hypertension and depression reported experiencing progressive generalized weakness, fatigability, mild nonspecific headaches, and confusion over the past 10 months. Her condition notably deteriorated in the week prior to her visit, leading to multiple falls. In the emergency department, she denied experiencing visual changes, seizures or seizure-like activity, any specific pattern to her headaches, nausea, vomiting, or other constitutional symptoms. Her neurological examination revealed no apparent focal neurological deficits and was within normal limits.
A 26-year-old Japanese male experienced severe headache and nausea for about 3 weeks. He had a previous episode that involved convulsion-like symptoms.

The patient is a 3-year-and-11-month-old female, the second child of healthy parents with a healthy 10-year-old elder brother. She was delivered via full-term cesarean section with a birth weight of 3300 g and a head circumference larger than the normal range. She exhibited hand deformities, including flexed hands and outward-tilting fingers that could not be extended. At 5 months, she was unable to look up or turn over. Following rehabilitation training, she could walk with support and say simple words like 'Mom' and 'Dad.' Rehabilitation training was discontinued thereafter. By age 3, she could walk and run independently but still only spoke a few simple words. Currently, her height is in the 97th percentile for her age group, and her weight exceeds the 97th percentile for children of the same age. She has experienced regression in language development and is unable to engage in routine communication. Her facial features include a protruding forehead, a head circumference of 57 cm, oblique cleft eyes, widely spaced eyes, a long mandibular tip, and hair thinning in both temporal areas. Except for the thumbs, the other four fingers on both hands are excessively outward, and her palms lack palm prints. The first seizure occurred at 3-and-a-half years old, characterized by cyanotic lips, dyspnea, stiffness, and fever, resolving spontaneously after 2–3 minutes.

A 37-year-old woman with a history of gestational diabetes was admitted following a motor vehicle accident for evaluation of recurrent low blood sugar levels. She initially experienced a loss of consciousness due to a witnessed seizure, which improved after receiving 5% dextrose (D5W) at the accident scene.
